caption:
Ben Franklin retired at 42. Not by luck. He ran a tracking system on himself: 13 virtues, one per week, a black spot for every fault, every night.

He failed at some of it. He admitted it. And still said the attempt made him a better and a happier man.

What's the one habit you'd track for 13 weeks?

Source: Franklin's Autobiography (ch. IX) and Harvard Magazine.

slides.heading: At 42, Ben Franklin quit working.
slides.body:
Not because he got lucky.

Because he ran a system on himself for years.

Here's the system. And the 200-year bet he left behind.

slides.heading: He retired with a 2-page contract.
slides.body:
In 1748 he gave 50% of his print shop to his foreman, David Hall.

Nobody could buy a business back then. No investors, no acquirers.

So he built the next best thing: a long-term passive income from the shop he no longer worked in.

slides.heading: The money part of his system.
slides.body:
FRUGALITY
"Make no expense but to do good to others or yourself; i.e., waste nothing."

INDUSTRY
"Lose no time; be always employed in something useful."

His own logic: these two clear your debt and give you "affluence and independence."

slides.heading: How he tracked it.
slides.body:
A little book. One page per virtue. Seven columns for the days of the week.

Every evening he marked a black spot for each fault.

One virtue per week. 13 weeks per round. Four rounds a year.

Not all at once. Like weeding a garden one bed at a time.

slides.heading: Where he failed: Order.
slides.body:
He called himself incorrigible at it.

He almost gave up, and told a story about a man who quit grinding his axe halfway: "I think I like a speckled ax best."

His point: most people quit a standard the moment it gets tiring, then call the compromise their preference.

slides.heading: The virtue he added later.
slides.body:
His list started with twelve.

A Quaker friend told him people thought he was proud and overbearing in arguments.

So he added Humility, and banned words like "certainly" and "undoubtedly" from his own mouth.

He said it made his ideas land easier, even though he was never a good speaker.

slides.heading: He never got it perfect.
slides.body:
He admitted he fell far short of perfection.

But he wrote that the attempt made him "a better and a happier man" than he'd have been without it.

He credited Industry and Frugality for his early financial ease.

slides.heading: Then came the 200-year bet.
slides.body:
In 1790 he left £1,000 each to Boston and Philadelphia.

The money was to be lent to young married tradesmen who'd finished their apprenticeships, at 5% over ten years.

His own math: about £4 million each after 200 years.

slides.heading: What actually happened.
slides.body:
By 1990, Philadelphia's fund was worth about $2 million. Boston's about $4.5 to $5 million.

Both cities drifted from his plan. Boston stopped the loans, Philadelphia fell well short of his projection.

Still: £1,000 turned into millions. Even badly managed.

slides.heading: His edge wasn't talent.
slides.body:
It was tracking.

One habit. One week. One mark every night.

What's the one thing you'd track for 13 weeks?
